I've been farming this land for 20 years. I know Quzhou's soil and water well. The groundwater level has been dropping every year, so I watch my irrigation carefully. My wheat-maize rotation fields are my foundation — reliable income. Cotton is getting harder to manage with rising labor costs, but I've done it for years and know how to handle it. Stevia is my bet on a better contract price this season.

Here's how I'm planning it:

My 600 mu breaks down like this: 300 mu in the wheat-maize double-crop rotation (same land, two seasons), 150 mu in cotton, and 150 mu in stevia. That's how I've run it the last few years and it covers my costs while spreading risk.

**Wheat (winter, 300 mu):** I'll use the improved variety — Jimai 22 or similar — nothing fancy but reliable. Rotary tillage after maize harvest to chop the stalks under. I'll apply base fertilizer before sowing, then topdress nitrogen at jointing. Four irrigations: pre-winter water, jointing, heading, and grain fill. Two pesticide passes — one for aphids, one for powdery mildew. Expecting around 450 kg/mu.

**Maize (summer, 300 mu):** Straight after wheat harvest, I go in with hybrid seed — Xianyu 335 or Zhengdan 958. No-tillage direct seeding to save time and moisture. Maize needs more nitrogen than wheat; I'll split it between base and side-dress at V6. Two to three irrigations depending on rainfall. Two pesticide applications for armyworm and corn borer. Expecting 550 kg/mu.

**Cotton (spring, 150 mu):** Hybrid Bt cotton — reduces my pesticide burden somewhat, but I still spray 5-6 times through the season. More irrigation than the grain crops. I plough this field in spring to prepare a good seedbed. Labor is my biggest cost here. Expecting 280 kg/mu seed cotton.

**Stevia (spring, 150 mu):** Improved cutting variety from my supplier. Stevia needs good potassium for leaf quality. I'll do rotary tillage, apply base fertilizer heavy on K, and irrigate 4 times. Light pesticide — 2 passes. Expecting 130 kg/mu dry leaves if the contract buyer grades it well.
